Chrome Extension Permission Checker

Scans your extension's JavaScript/TypeScript source for chrome.* API usage and checks it against manifest.json's declared permissions, optional_permissions, and host_permissions -- the most common cause of a Chrome Web Store review rejection for excessive or unused permissions ("Purple Potassium"), plus the reverse case: an API call whose permission was never declared, which fails at runtime. Everything runs in this tab; nothing is uploaded. A command-line version for CI is in the same repository (node check.mjs .).


Open your extension's project folder, select every .js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx file plus manifest.json (select-all works), then choose them here. Not at your project right now? instead.

No files selected yet.

Common questions

Why did Chrome Web Store reject my extension for unused or excessive permissions (Purple Potassium)?

Chrome's own troubleshooting documentation names this as the most common review rejection: your manifest.json declares a permission that reviewers cannot find a matching feature for. This tool scans your source for the chrome.* calls each permission unlocks and tells you exactly which declared permission has no detected use.

What does it mean if my extension uses a chrome.* API that isn't declared in the manifest?

That call will fail at runtime, not just at review -- Chrome enforces the permission at the API level. This tool checks both directions: permissions declared but unused, and APIs used but undeclared.

Is my extension's source code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser tool reads the files you select using the File API and never sends them anywhere -- everything happens in memory in your tab. The CLI never makes a network call either.

Does a clean report mean Chrome Web Store will approve my extension?

No. This is evidence of what your code and your manifest currently say, produced by pattern-matching known chrome.* symbols -- it is not the review process, and it cannot see permissions used only by a bundled third-party library's minified code, dynamic imports, or a permission the manifest declares with no code signature this tool maps (activeTab, background, unlimitedStorage, and ChromeOS/enterprise-only permissions). Always confirm against Chrome's current documentation before submitting.

More on the specific rejection code: Fixing "Purple Potassium" unused-permission rejections.

Vetting an extension someone else already published instead of your own? See this checker vs. CRXcavator. Prefer to just read the manifest? See this checker vs. checking the manifest by hand.

Evidence, not a determination. This tool reports what pattern-matching found in the files you selected and what your manifest declares. It cannot see a permission used only inside a bundled third-party library's minified code, a dynamic import, or a permission with no code signature this tool maps. A clean report is not a guarantee Chrome Web Store review will pass -- verify against Chrome's current documentation before you submit, and remove or justify each permission based on what your extension actually does.

It is not legal advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or Chrome Web Store's own review process. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. Nothing leaves your browser. Files you select are read locally with the File API and never uploaded. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day -- no file names, no file contents, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Building a WordPress plugin too? WordPress Plugin Review Checker cross-checks a readme.txt Stable tag against the plugin header's Version -- the same "read a manifest you already have, name the exact mismatch" shape as this tool, for wordpress.org Plugin Review.

purple-potassium-unused-permissions.html.text:
Fixing "Purple Potassium" unused-permission rejections

Purple Potassium is the internal name Chrome Web Store review uses for a rejection about excessive or unused permissions in manifest.json. Google's own troubleshooting documentation calls requesting a permission you don't actually need the single most common rejection reason for the platform. It applies to both the named API permissions in permissions/optional_permissions and to broad host_permissions patterns like <all_urls>.

Why it happens

A reviewer -- or an automated pre-check -- compares your declared permissions against what your extension's code and UI actually appear to do, and cannot find a feature that needs one of them. This is easy to trigger by accident: a permission left over from a removed feature, one copied from a tutorial or boilerplate, or one requested "just in case" for a feature not yet built.

The two shapes of the problem

ShapeWhat it meansCost
Declared, not usedA permission sits in the manifest with no matching chrome.* call anywhereReview rejection (Purple Potassium)
Used, not declaredCode calls a chrome.* API whose permission was never added to the manifestRuntime failure -- the call throws or silently no-ops, independent of review

Find the exact permission

The checker on this site scans your source for the namespace each permission unlocks (chrome.storage for storage, chrome.tabs for tabs, and more than 40 others), reads your manifest, and reports both directions -- declared-but-unused and used-but-undeclared -- plus any broad host_permissions pattern, with the exact file and line for every match it can find. It runs as a browser tool (nothing uploaded) or a Node CLI you can add to your own pre-submission check.

This is evidence of what the code and the manifest say, not a determination that Chrome Web Store review will pass -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it can and can't see (bundled third-party library code and dynamic imports in particular), and verify against Chrome's current documentation before you resubmit.

vs-checking-the-manifest-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to Chrome Extension Permission Checker

Chrome Extension Permission Checker vs. checking the manifest by hand

Reading manifest.json alongside your source and searching for each declared permission's API calls genuinely works, and it is the method most extension developers already use before a submission. This page names no product or company being compared against: "checking the manifest by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseChecking the manifest by handThis tool
A permission with one obvious code shape, e.g. chrome.storage.*Correctly caught by a search for the patternCorrectly caught the same way
clipboardRead, which is either navigator.clipboard.readText() or document.execCommand('paste')Searching for one pattern and not finding it reads as "unused" even when the other is presentChecks both known signatures for every permission that has more than one
A host pattern listed inside permissions rather than a separate host_permissions array (Manifest V2 style)Easy to skim past as an ordinary API permission entryReads a host pattern wherever it appears and checks it against the same broad-pattern set
A newly added chrome.* call whose permission was never added to the manifestRequires diffing the whole source tree against the manifest again after every changeRe-scans every file given each run, regardless of which one changed
A permission with no checkable code signature (ChromeOS/enterprise-only)No way to tell "not checked" from "confirmed unused" without reading the tool's own documentationReports these explicitly as not checked rather than guessing

The gap that matters most: more than one code shape per permission

Not every permission has a single, unambiguous API call to search for. clipboardRead is unlocked by either the modern navigator.clipboard.readText() or the older document.execCommand('paste'), and a codebase can use either. A developer who searches for only one and comes up empty will report the permission unused -- the wrong conclusion if the other pattern is what the code actually uses. This tool checks every known signature for a permission, not just the one a developer happened to think of first.

The gap that matters second: a host pattern hiding among API permissions

Manifest V2 extensions often list broad site-access patterns directly inside the permissions array next to ordinary API permissions like storage and tabs, with nothing to visually distinguish them. A skim for suspicious chrome.* usage has no reason to single out an entry that is not an API permission at all. This tool checks every host-shaped entry it finds, in either array, against the same fixed broad-pattern list every time.

When to still read the manifest yourself

This tool answers whether a permission's code signature is present or absent in the source you point it at -- it has no opinion on whether the feature behind that signature is worth the scrutiny a broad permission invites in review, and Chrome Web Store review ultimately judges justification, not just presence. Deciding whether a permission is actually needed, and writing the justification review will ask for, is still a job for you.

Common questions

What does checking the manifest by hand actually catch?

A developer who remembers to look can spot an obviously unused permission -- a leftover storage entry from a feature that got removed, say -- by scanning the source for chrome.storage. and not finding it. That review genuinely works for a small codebase with permissions whose API surface is a single, obvious pattern, which is most of them.

Why does a permission like clipboardRead slip past a manual search?

clipboardRead has two unrelated code shapes that both use it: the modern navigator.clipboard.readText() call, and the older document.execCommand('paste'). A developer searching the source for one pattern and not finding it will conclude the permission is unused, when the code actually uses the other pattern. This tool checks both signatures for every permission that has more than one, so which one a codebase happens to use never matters.

Why is telling a host pattern apart from an API permission easy to get wrong by eye?

Manifest V2 extensions commonly list host patterns like *://*.example.com/* directly inside the permissions array, alongside ordinary API permissions like storage and tabs -- there is no separate host_permissions array to signal which entries are which. A developer skimming the array for chrome.* API misuse has no visual cue that one entry is a broad site-access grant rather than an API permission, and might not think to check it against the broad-pattern list at all. This tool reads a host pattern wherever it appears -- in permissions or the newer host_permissions array -- and checks it against the same fixed broad-pattern set every time.

Why is re-checking the whole source tree easy to skip?

A used-but-undeclared permission -- code calling a chrome.* API whose permission was never added to the manifest -- fails at runtime, independent of review, and catching it means diffing every file against the manifest again after every change. That is easy to skip on a routine feature addition, especially right before a submission deadline when a developer is focused on the one file they just edited. This tool re-scans every file it is given every time, so a permission gap introduced anywhere in the tree is caught the same way regardless of which file changed.

Does this replace deciding whether a permission is actually justified?

No. This tool answers whether a permission's code signature is present or absent -- it has no opinion on whether the feature that signature supports is worth the review scrutiny a broad permission invites. Chrome Web Store review ultimately judges justification, not just presence, and that judgment call is still yours.

Evidence, not a determination. This is pattern-matching against known chrome.* API signatures in the source you point it at. A clean report describes what that scan found, not a guarantee a Chrome Web Store review will pass.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It does not replace reading Chrome's own permissions documentation. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence -- support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-crxcavator.html.text:
← Chrome extension permission checker

This checker vs. CRXcavator

CRXcavator, from Duo Security (now part of Cisco), takes a Chrome Web Store extension ID -- or an uploaded .crx file -- and produces a risk score from the packaged extension's requested permissions, Content Security Policy, retire.js findings, and webstore listing metadata. It is aimed at a security or IT team deciding whether an extension someone else built and published is safe to allow.

This checker is a different job entirely. It is a free, zero-dependency tool -- usable in the browser with no upload, or as a Node CLI -- that reads your own extension's source tree and its manifest.json, before you have submitted anything to the Chrome Web Store. It scans for chrome.* API calls in your JavaScript/TypeScript and cross-checks them against the permissions, optional_permissions, and host_permissions your manifest declares, naming any declared-but-unused permission (Google's documentation cites this as the most common review rejection, "Purple Potassium") and any API call whose permission was never declared (a runtime failure, not just a review problem).

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Decide whether to trust an already-published extension you did not write, for your own use or your organization's. CRXcavator -- it scans the published .crx and webstore listing and returns a risk score, no source access needed.
Find out why your own unpublished extension might get rejected for an unused permission, or fail at runtime on a missing one. This checker -- it reads your source and manifest directly, before you submit anything.
Score an extension's Content Security Policy, webstore rating, or third-party library versions. CRXcavator -- none of that is something this checker looks at; it is permissions only.
Reconcile a manifest against the code behind it, line by line, with no publish step and nothing uploaded. This checker -- the browser tool reads local files with the File API and never sends them anywhere; the CLI makes no network call.
Vet a list of extensions already installed across an organization's browsers. CRXcavator -- it is built for exactly that fleet-review use case; this checker has no fleet or inventory feature.

These fit different points in an extension's life rather than competing for the same one. A team building its own extension can run this checker before every submission to catch a permission mismatch early, and separately run something like CRXcavator over the third-party extensions it is deciding whether to trust. Neither replaces the other.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or CRXcavator?

They look at extensions from opposite sides. CRXcavator, built by Duo Security (now part of Cisco), takes a Chrome Web Store extension ID or an uploaded .crx and produces a risk score from its packaged code, requested permissions, Content Security Policy, and webstore metadata -- it is built for a security or IT team deciding whether to trust an extension someone else published. This checker takes your own extension's source tree and manifest.json, before you have published anything, and cross-checks the chrome.* APIs your code actually calls against the permissions you declared. Reach for CRXcavator when you are vetting a third-party extension you did not write. Reach for this when you are the one writing the extension and want to catch a 'Purple Potassium' unused-permission rejection, or a missing permission that would fail at runtime, before you submit.

CRXcavator is free too. What does this add?

Being free is not the difference, and this page does not claim it is: CRXcavator is a free tool. The difference is what each one needs and what it can see. CRXcavator needs a published extension -- it scans the packaged .crx and the Chrome Web Store listing, so it cannot run against an extension that only exists on your disk. This checker needs your source and your manifest, and nothing else: no upload, no Chrome Web Store listing, no publish step first. It is built for the moment before you have anything to submit, which is exactly the moment a risk-scoring tool for already-listed extensions cannot help with.

If CRXcavator already scores permissions, why run a permission-only checker?

Because they answer different questions about permissions. CRXcavator's score tells a reviewer or an IT team how much access an already-published extension is asking for, weighed against its other signals -- useful for deciding whether to allow it. This checker tells the developer of an unpublished extension which specific declared permission has no matching chrome.* call in their own code (the exact shape of Chrome's most-cited rejection reason) and, in the other direction, which API call has no permission declared for it at all, which is a runtime failure waiting to happen. A risk score is a verdict about trustworthiness; this is a line-by-line reconciliation between a manifest and the code behind it.

Is this page affiliated with Cisco or Duo Security?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Cisco Systems or Duo Security, and CRXcavator is named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. The description of CRXcavator on this page is drawn from its own public site; check it there for what it currently scores and how.
